column1: What is the core invariant governing iron-sight marksmanship regarding angular vs. linear error?
column2: A small angular error at the sighting plane (sight alignment) produces a large linear error at distance; the sight radius acts as mechanical leverage against this angular error.

column1: Why does a pistol with a 150mm sight radius tolerate alignment errors worse than a rifle with a 500mm sight radius?
column2: A longer sight radius reduces the angular displacement produced by the same linear sight error, so the same 0.5mm front sight offset produces less angular (and thus linear downrange) deviation on the rifle.

column1: During the moment of discharge, where should visual focus be placed and why?
column2: On the front sight, not the target — because the eye cannot focus at two distances simultaneously, and the front sight is the last controllable mechanical variable before the bullet leaves the barrel.

column1: What is the 'surprise break' principle in trigger control?
column2: The trigger finger applies steady, continuous rearward pressure without rhythmic hesitation or surge, so the exact instant of sear release remains temporally unpredictable to the shooter's own anticipatory reflexes, preventing flinch.

column1: What physiological phenomenon causes 'anticipation' flinch, and what is its characteristic effect on point of impact?
column2: A brainstem-driven protective flinch response to the concussive report/recoil (occurring ~300ms before conscious thought) causes a downward push of the muzzle just before firing, resulting in shots breaking low and off to one side.

column1: Why is anticipation (flinch) particularly dangerous to diagnose via the shooter's own feedback?
column2: Because it feels correct from the inside — the shooter often reports a smooth trigger press and steady sight picture even while flinching enough to move the muzzle several inches at distance.

column1: What is 'mechanical isolation' in trigger control?
column2: The ability to move the trigger finger through its full range of travel without introducing movement in any adjacent structure (hand, wrist, or grip).

column1: What is the dividing line between internal and external ballistics?
column2: The muzzle crown — internal ballistics ends and external ballistics begins the instant the projectile clears the muzzle.

column1: Why do a 175-grain .308 bullet and a 300-grain .338 bullet fall at the same rate under gravity?
column2: Gravity accelerates all bullets downward at 32.174 ft/s² regardless of mass, shape, or velocity, so only reducing time of flight (via speed or drag reduction) can counter it.

column1: What does dialing elevation into a scope actually accomplish, physically?
column2: It angles the bore upward so the bullet's arcing path passes through the target's height at the moment it reaches the target's distance — it does not counteract gravity directly, it's a time-of-flight correction expressed in angular units.

column1: Why is a bullet's trajectory asymmetric (not a symmetric parabola) in air?
column2: Aerodynamic drag is proportional to velocity squared and decelerates the bullet continuously, so it spends more time in the descending half of the trajectory; the apex shifts to roughly 55-60% of the distance to target.

column1: What three immutable physical principles underlie platform integration in tactical shooting?
column2: 1) The shooter-weapon interface acts as a coupled mechanical oscillator; 2) weapon ergonomics (e.g., length of pull, bore-to-sight offset) constrain biomechanical efficiency; 3) performance degrades nonlinearly under physiological stress (fine motor control fails >145 BPM, cognitive tunneling at 175 BPM, complex motor patterns fail above 200 BPM).
